summary: Defines a template for the QSPEC object, which carries QoS model specific information in the QoS NSLP, and a set of QSPEC parameters. They provide a common language across models like IntServ or Diffserv. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: QSPEC gives QoS NSLP messages a common format for describing traffic and service requirements. Network nodes can update available-resource information or translate the request for a local QoS model.

questions: how does qspec encode qos requirements
how do qspec parameters travel across domain boundaries
subtitle: A template for carrying quality-of-service requirements in QoS NSLP messages.

tldr.problem: QoS NSLP signals reservations across network domains that may use different QoS models and terminology. Those domains need a common way to describe requested, available and reserved service.
tldr.mechanism: QSPEC defines four object types and reusable parameters, including a mandatory traffic model. Nodes process the parameters, update available-resource information and may translate the request into a local QSPEC for a domain.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5975 is Experimental. Its template supports shared QoS signaling, but each network's QoS model determines how resources are managed.

today: RFC 5975 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard. The RFC metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: QSPEC and Different QoS Models
sections.content:
QoS NSLP signals resource reservations for a data flow. It is independent of a particular QoS model, while the QSPEC object carries the model-specific information that resource-management functions need.

A QSPEC can include an end-to-end Initiator QSPEC. At a domain boundary, a node may translate it into a Local QSPEC and keep the Initiator QSPEC inside it, so the local domain can process its own parameters while preserving the original request.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS NSLP carries reservation messages, and QSPEC carries the service details inside them. This separation lets different network domains use their own resource-management methods.

sections.title: Four QSPEC Objects
sections.content:
A QSPEC can contain QoS Desired, QoS Available, QoS Reserved and Minimum QoS objects. QoS Desired describes what the initiator requests. QoS Available collects information about resources along the path, and QoS Reserved reports the resources actually reserved.

Minimum QoS lets an initiator specify the least acceptable service. If available resources fall below the stated minimum, the reservation fails. A QSPEC can contain only the objects needed for its message sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: The four objects describe what is requested, what the path can provide, what was reserved and the minimum the requester accepts. A message can use only some of them.

sections.title: Traffic and Path Parameters
sections.content:
The Traffic Model (TMOD) parameter is mandatory. It describes traffic with five values: rate, bucket size, peak rate, minimum policed unit and maximum packet size. Other parameters can describe path latency, jitter, packet loss ratio, packet error ratio, priorities, excess-traffic treatment and traffic classification.

The initiator marks a parameter as mandatory to interpret with the M flag. A node that cannot interpret a mandatory parameter causes the reservation to fail. A node may ignore an unknown parameter when the M flag is not set.
sections.plainLanguage: TMOD describes the flow's traffic pattern, and optional parameters describe path limits or handling instructions. The M flag tells downstream nodes that they must understand a parameter.

sections.title: Processing Requests and Reporting Results
sections.content:
Each QoS NSIS Entity (QNE) processes the QSPEC according to its resource-management function. A QNE may update QoS Available as the request moves along the path. It can set an error flag when a requested resource is unavailable, or a not-supported flag when it cannot interpret a parameter.

The RFC describes sender-initiated reservations, receiver-initiated transactions and resource queries. A response reports whether the reservation succeeded and may return the available or reserved values. Local QSPEC parameters are translated at a domain edge and removed when the message leaves that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node checks the request against its local resources and updates the information about what is available. Responses tell the initiator whether the reservation succeeded and what the path could provide.

sections.title: Priority and Security
sections.content:
QSPEC security depends on QoS NSLP security. The RFC highlights a risk in priority parameters: a user could falsely claim emergency priority and prevent genuine emergency calls from getting through.

The RFC suggests restricting emergency priority to authorized user groups or allowing it only for particular destination addresses. These controls are examples of protections against misuse of priority.
sections.plainLanguage: A user could falsely label traffic as an emergency and take resources from real emergency calls. Networks can restrict which users or destinations may use emergency priority.
